description: AUSTROX is an intelligent astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to track and analyse health changes before, during, and after space missions. It monitors muscle loss, bone density, mobility, ageing-related effects, and other physiological changes. Using AI, sensors, and predictive analytics, AUSTROX aims to identify health risks early, support preventive measures, improve recovery, and uncover hidden insights into how space environments affect the human body.
summary: AUSTROX is an intelligent astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to address one of the biggest challenges of long-duration space exploration: protecting human health beyond Earth.From Earth to orbit, the Moon and Mars, AUSTROX provides continuous, location-aware monitoring of an astronaut's physical and behavioural health. It brings together vital signs, bone density, muscle mass, mobility, radiation exposure, sleep and stress into one unified platform.Its key innovation is combining 3D movement and gait analysis with personalised health baselines and predictive modelling. By understanding the gravitational and environmental conditions astronauts experience, it identifies unusual changes, forecasts potential health risks, tracks the impact of exercise countermeasures and provides clear alerts with actionable recommendations.Designed around astronaut autonomy, the platform aims to support early intervention and informed health decisions, even when communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable.AUSTROX covers the entire mission lifecycle before, during and after spaceflight helping monitor individual health changes, support recovery and improve preparedness for future deep-space missions.Built as a working web prototype with simulated sensor streams, interactive visualisations and predictive demonstrations, AUSTROX aims to contribute to safer human space exploration while opening possibilities for applications in rehabilitation, ageing and remote healthcare on Earth.

AUSTROX: Submission Dossier

Intelligent astronaut health monitoring for Earth, orbit, the Moon and Mars

Team AUSTROX | NASA Space Apps Challenge | Live platform: https://austrox.netlify.app

How to use this document. Part A is ready to paste into the submission form. Part B explains each health problem with official data, how AUSTROX solves it, and how NASA can lead on it. Parts C to F cover what makes the project unique, honest limits, a pitch script and judge Q&A. Part G lists every source link so judges can verify the numbers.

PART A: SUBMISSION CONTENT

A1. Project at a glance

Field

Entry

Project name

AUSTROX

Challenge

Astronaut health monitoring: gather health indicators and let astronauts evaluate and act on their health status on long-duration missions

One-line pitch

A 24/7, location-aware AI monitor that tracks muscle, bone, mobility, ageing and radiation effects and warns astronauts early

Live website

https://austrox.netlify.app

Team

Team AUSTROX

Status

Working web prototype with live simulated sensor streams, 3D motion analysis, forecasts and a self-check tool

A2. Short summary (about 60 words)

AUSTROX is an intelligent astronaut health-monitoring platform. It follows an astronaut before, during and after a mission, whether on Earth, in orbit, on the Moon or on Mars. Wearable-style sensors, AI movement recognition and predictive analytics track bone density, muscle mass, mobility, radiation dose and stress, then raise early warnings and recommend actions the astronaut can take immediately.

A3. Full project description

Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, a closed environment and distance from Earth. NASA's Human Research Program groups these as five hazards linked to more than 30 documented health risks. On a trip to Mars, help from Earth can be 20 minutes away each way, so astronauts must be able to spot and act on changes in their own bodies.

AUSTROX is the single monitor built for that situation. It keeps tracking around the clock and is aware of where the astronaut is. Gravity and radiation levels for Earth (1 g), the ISS (about 0 g), the Moon (0.165 g) and Mars (0.38 g) change what the system expects to see, how it judges gait, and how fast it forecasts bone and muscle change.

The platform combines five layers: (1) continuous vitals such as heart rate, blood oxygen, HRV, temperature and sleep; (2) a location-aware environment model; (3) a movement recognition engine that rebuilds the astronaut as a 3D skeleton and measures speed, cadence, stride length and gait symmetry; (4) predictive analytics that forecast bone and muscle change with and without exercise countermeasures; and (5) a 0 to 100 health risk index with plain-language alerts and an astronaut self-evaluation tool for sleep, mood, pain and balance.

A4. What it does

  • Streams eight health indicators every second and draws live trend lines.
  • Switches between Earth, ISS orbit, Moon and Mars and re-computes every metric for that environment.
  • Recognises movement type and speed (stationary, walking, brisk walking, running) and analyses gait against the local gravity.
  • Forecasts bone density and muscle mass over a 500-day mission and shows the benefit of the exercise protocol.
  • Tracks cumulative radiation dose against NASA career limits.
  • Produces one risk score and specific alerts, such as bone loss above 3% or muscle loss above 5%.
  • Lets the astronaut log how they feel and returns an instant action plan, including an urgent flag to contact ground support.

A5. How we built it

  • Front end: HTML5, CSS and JavaScript with Canvas rendering for the 3D globe, starfield, skeleton pose and charts. Hosted at https://austrox.netlify.app.
  • Environment model: gravity and radiation constants per location, scaled from published loss rates (about 1 to 1.5% bone loss per month in weight-bearing bones without countermeasures).
  • Motion engine: a 3D skeleton whose gait changes with speed and gravity (walking on Earth, bounding on the Moon, floating in orbit).
  • Analytics: per-astronaut baselines and trend forecasting, with a what-if switch for the exercise protocol.
  • Planned: real wearable inputs (IMU, ECG, SpO2, dosimeter), on-board edge AI that works offline, and a flight-surgeon dashboard.

A6. NASA and public data used

The model constants and the evidence section of the website are based on public NASA Human Research Program material, the NASA Twins Study, peer-reviewed spaceflight papers and 2026 news coverage. Full links are in Part G. Live sensor values in the prototype are simulated and are labelled as such on the site.

A7. Challenges we faced

  • Combining very different body systems into one understandable risk score.
  • Making the same interface correct for four different gravity and radiation environments.
  • Showing 3D motion analysis in a lightweight browser page that works on any device.
  • Being honest about what is simulated and what is evidence-based.

A8. What we are proud of

  • A complete, working, shareable platform that judges can open from a link or QR code.
  • Movement recognition tied to gravity, which most health dashboards do not offer.
  • Every claim in the evidence section is tied to an official or peer-reviewed source.

A9. What we learned

Astronaut health is a connected system: bone, muscle, fluids, immunity, sleep and mood affect each other. The Twins Study showed that one astronaut's changes were highly individual, which is why personal baselines matter more than population averages.

A10. What is next

Connect real wearable sensors, train anomaly models on open NASA datasets such as the Open Science Data Repository, test offline edge deployment, add a flight-surgeon dashboard, and validate forecasts against published ISS and bed-rest data.

PART B: EVERY PROBLEM, THE OFFICIAL DATA, AND HOW AUSTROX SOLVES IT

B1. NASA's framework: five hazards

Official position. NASA's Human Research Program (HRP) has identified five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile or closed environments. A peer-reviewed review states these hazards are linked to over 30 human health risks documented by HRP. NASA also states the hazards do not stand alone, so they interact.

How AUSTROX answers it. AUSTROX is organised around the same hazards. Location drives gravity and radiation, the self-check covers isolation and behavioural strain, on-board AI covers distance from Earth, and the risk index shows how hazards combine instead of treating each in isolation.

Verify: NASA: Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight | Peer-reviewed overview (PMC) | Human Research Roadmap

B2. Problem 1: Bone loss

The issue. NASA states that without an effective countermeasure astronauts lose bone density at 1 to 2% per month, which may lead to early-onset osteoporosis and a higher fracture risk after returning to gravity. A NASA presentation on cosmonaut and astronaut scans gives site-specific rates: about 1.5% per month at the hip, 1% per month at the lumbar spine and 0.3% per month for the whole body. Urinary calcium excretion rises by 60 to 70% within the first days of microgravity. The Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED) is the first device shown to reduce, but not eliminate, bone loss and muscle deconditioning. A 2023 study of 46 ISS astronauts found longer missions were generally associated with greater loss of bone content.

Why it matters. Loss is fast, site-specific and may not fully recover. Mars missions are longer than ISS stays, so the loss accumulates and crews land in a gravity field where fractures are possible.

How AUSTROX solves it. The bone density index is updated continuously from location gravity, mission day and exercise compliance. The forecast chart shows the expected curve to day 500 with and without the protocol, and an alert fires when loss passes 3% of baseline. The astronaut sees the exact value of the exercise protocol in percentage points and can adjust before damage builds up.

How NASA can lead. NASA can use continuous, per-astronaut bone-risk forecasts to tailor exercise prescriptions and decide when pharmaceutical support is needed. NASA's own research already compares exercise with drugs for bone protection, and a live tracker closes the loop between the protocol and the result.

Verify: NASA Sibonga bone presentation (NTRS) | Sibonga et al., Bone 2019 | npj Microgravity 2023, 46 astronauts

B3. Problem 2: Muscle atrophy and loss of strength

The issue. A meta-analysis of spaceflight studies found that current exercise countermeasures are insufficient to eliminate loss of lower-body muscle function and mass during long missions. Muscle mass is lost at roughly 0.57% per month on average, and mainly in the legs, with arm muscle largely unchanged. On the ISS, crews exercise about 600 minutes per week each. Early shuttle flights without modern countermeasures reported losses of up to about 20% of muscle mass within 5 to 11 days; this figure comes from secondary literature, so cite the primary study if you present it as a headline.

Why it matters. Muscle is the engine of every surface task: walking on Mars, climbing out of a lander, carrying equipment. Weak legs on arrival is a mission-safety risk.

How AUSTROX solves it. The muscle mass index is tracked per astronaut, and the movement engine adds a second signal: gait symmetry and stride length. A falling symmetry score is an early sign of muscle imbalance before the strength test shows it. Alerts fire at 5% muscle loss and when the exercise protocol is switched off.

How NASA can lead. Wearable motion data can become a daily, no-test strength proxy so crews do not need dedicated testing sessions, and can feed NASA's work on individual exercise prescription.

Verify: Exercise countermeasures meta-analysis (PMC) | npj Microgravity 2023

B4. Problem 3: Space radiation

The issue. NASA calls radiation one of the most hazardous aspects of spaceflight, with risks including cancer and central nervous system damage. The National Academies recommended a single career limit of about 600 mSv for all astronauts, aimed at keeping cancer-death risk at or below 3%. The same report says long missions to Mars are likely to significantly exceed that limit, so waivers would be needed unless protection improves. Reporting on the report notes a six-month lunar surface stay could mean nearly 200 mSv, and a full Mars voyage could exceed 1,000 mSv. Curiosity's radiation detector measured the cruise-phase environment on the way to Mars.

Why it matters. Radiation dose is a budget that cannot be refilled. Where the astronaut is and how long they stay decide how much of the career limit is spent.

How AUSTROX solves it. Radiation rates are built into each location (ISS about 0.5 mSv per day, Moon about 1.3, Mars about 0.7 on the surface and about 1.8 in transit). The monitor tracks cumulative dose against the career limit and warns when the budget is shrinking, so crews and planners can use shielded rest areas and storm shelters earlier.

How NASA can lead. A personal dose ledger that moves with the astronaut supports the exact waiver decisions the National Academies describes, because each person's remaining budget is known at any time.

Verify: National Academies report summary | Scientific American | Curiosity cruise radiation, Science 2013 | Mars surface radiation, Science 2014

B5. Problem 4: Fluid shift, cardiovascular and eye changes

The issue. In the NASA Twins Study, Scott Kelly's carotid artery wall thickened early in the 340-day mission and stayed thickened. The headward fluid shift also distended the jugular vein and was linked to Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), with a thickened retinal nerve layer and folds in the choroid. NASA lists SANS, fluid shifts and cardiovascular deconditioning among its recognised long-term risks.

Why it matters. These changes affect vision and circulation, which are mission-critical, and some may not reverse.

How AUSTROX solves it. Heart rate, HRV and blood oxygen trends are logged continuously, and the self-check asks about dizziness and balance. Combined with location and mission day, the risk index rises when cardiovascular indicators drift from the personal baseline.

How NASA can lead. Continuous cardiovascular trends give flight surgeons an early flag for when to use limited onboard ultrasound and imaging time.

Verify: NASA Twins Study results | Science 2019 paper

B6. Problem 5: Immune and molecular stress

The issue. NASA's HRP notes stress hormones are elevated in space, which can alter immune function and increase susceptibility to illness. In the Twins Study, more than 1,000 genes changed expression as soon as Scott arrived in space, linked to DNA repair and immune response. His telomeres lengthened in flight, then shortened after return, leaving more short telomeres than before. Most changes returned to baseline within about six months, but some immune-related genes stayed overactive. NASA concluded the study supports the need for personalised medicine in deep space.

Why it matters. Responses are highly individual, so population averages will miss early warning signs in a specific person.

How AUSTROX solves it. The platform is built around the individual's own baseline. Pre-mission Earth data becomes the reference line, and every in-flight and post-flight measurement is compared with that person, not with a generic range.

How NASA can lead. A per-astronaut baseline across the whole mission arc gives NASA structured data for the personalised approach the Twins Study recommended.

Verify: NASA Twins Study results | Space.com on NASA's HRP risks

B7. Problem 6: Isolation, confinement and behavioural health

The issue. NASA's HRP says behavioural issues are inevitable when groups are confined in small spaces for long periods, and expects a Mars trip to be mentally demanding, with heavy workload alternating with boredom. NASA stresses that lighting, movement and sleep are important for isolated crews. On the ISS, the orbit creates 16 sunrises and sunsets in 24 hours, which disrupts circadian rhythm. In the Twins Study, cognitive speed and accuracy dropped after landing and persisted for up to six months.

Why it matters. Mood and sleep problems are early, silent signals that precede errors and conflict.

How AUSTROX solves it. The sleep quality indicator, HRV as a stress signal, and the daily self-check (sleep, mood, pain, balance) produce plain-language actions such as protecting an 8-hour rest window or requesting a call with the behavioural health team.

How NASA can lead. NASA is already researching early detection of impaired mental functioning; always-on passive indicators plus a quick self-report make that detection continuous.

Verify: Space.com on isolation and confinement | Space.com on ISS healthcare

B8. Problem 7: Distance from Earth and medical autonomy

The issue. NASA's HRP states communication between Mars and Earth will have a delay of about 20 minutes each way. In January 2026 NASA carried out the first medical evacuation in the ISS's 25 years of continuous crewed operations: Crew-11 returned about a month early after astronaut Mike Fincke had a sudden episode on 7 January that left him briefly unable to speak. The crew splashed down off San Diego on 15 January. The onboard ultrasound was used, but the advanced imaging needed was only available on Earth, and months later the cause was still unexplained. Modelling cited by Space.com suggests a medical emergency could be expected about every three years on the ISS, and exercise, the main countermeasure for bone and muscle, is now the leading source of injuries on the ISS.

Why it matters. On the ISS, a landing site is hours away. On the Moon it is days, and on Mars it is months. The crew must manage health on their own.

How AUSTROX solves it. On-board edge AI is designed to run offline: it detects anomalies, tracks trends and recommends actions without waiting for ground contact. The astronaut gets the status and the next step immediately, and ground teams get a clean summary when contact is available.

How NASA can lead. NASA can make autonomous health triage a standard part of Artemis and Mars vehicles, with risk indicators that decide whether a situation needs urgent return, treatment on board or monitoring.

Verify: HealthDay on the first ISS medical evacuation | Space.com analysis | Scripps News follow-up

B9. Problem 8: Changing gravity, balance and mobility

The issue. NASA's HRP says each change from one gravitational field to another affects hand-eye coordination, balance, movement and sense of space. Astronauts will move through Earth gravity, microgravity in transit, then Moon or Mars gravity and back. Scott Kelly reported dizziness, joint and muscle pain and swelling in the lower legs in his first days back on Earth.

Why it matters. Falls and injuries on arrival, or on return, can compromise a mission or a recovery.

How AUSTROX solves it. The movement recognition engine tracks speed, cadence, stride length and gait symmetry for the specific gravity. The system expects a bounding gait on the Moon, reduced-gravity walking on Mars and floating in orbit, and flags deviations. Post-mission, the same tracking measures recovery toward the pre-flight baseline.

How NASA can lead. Gait data is an objective measure of rehabilitation progress and readiness for surface tasks, and it needs no extra testing time.

Verify: Space.com on gravity transitions | Twins Study reporting (STAT)

PART C: HOW AUSTROX WORKS

C1. Five-step flow

  1. Wearables: IMU, ECG, SpO2, skin temperature and dosimeter.
  2. Location context: gravity and radiation model for Earth, ISS, Moon and Mars.
  3. Edge AI: on-board gait and anomaly detection that works offline.
  4. Predictive models: personal baselines and trend forecasts.
  5. Astronaut and ground: alerts, action plans and a flight-surgeon dashboard.

C3. Mission phases covered

  • Before the mission: an Earth baseline of vitals, strength, gait and bone indicators for each astronaut.
  • During the mission: continuous tracking, forecasts, alerts and daily self-evaluation.
  • After the mission: recovery tracking against the baseline, including gait symmetry and readjustment after landing.
PART D: WHAT MAKES AUSTROX DIFFERENT

NASA currently monitors astronaut health mainly through periodic tests and samples, such as fine motor skills, fluid distribution, fitness, vision and blood and urine samples. AUSTROX adds a continuous, location-aware, astronaut-facing layer on top. The comparison below describes the typical approach to our knowledge; it is not a claim about any specific system.

Our five unique selling points:

  1. Location-aware monitoring: the same body is judged differently on the Moon than on Mars.
  2. Movement-speed recognition as a health biomarker: gait becomes a daily, no-test measure of muscle and balance.
  3. Astronaut-first design: the challenge asks that astronauts evaluate and act on their own status, so AUSTROX gives them the tools and the next step.
  4. Countermeasure what-if forecasting: it shows the exact payoff of exercise in percentage points.
  5. One unified risk index: it connects hazards instead of listing them separately.
PART E: USES, BENEFICIARIES AND NASA ALIGNMENT
  • Astronauts: an instant, understandable view of their own health and what to do next.
  • Flight surgeons: a trend summary instead of raw data, when contact is available.
  • Mission planners: radiation and bone-loss budgets for crew selection and mission length.
  • NASA programmes: supports the HRP Mars-forward approach and Artemis lunar missions through personalised countermeasures and medical autonomy.
  • Earth benefits: bone and muscle loss in space resembles disuse and ageing on Earth. Bed-rest studies are used as analogs for microgravity, and healthy volunteers on strict bed rest lose roughly 1 to 1.5% of weight-bearing bone density per month. The same monitoring approach can support elderly care, rehabilitation, osteoporosis and sarcopenia monitoring and remote healthcare.
PART F: HONESTY, LIMITS, PITCH AND JUDGE Q&A

F1. Transparency statement (include in the submission)

The live sensor values in the AUSTROX prototype are simulated to demonstrate the interface and models. Forecast curves are illustrative and scaled from published loss rates. AUSTROX is a research and demonstration prototype and is not a medical device or medical advice. The next step is validation with real wearable data and published ISS and bed-rest datasets.

F2. Two-minute pitch script

0:00 Hook. "In January 2026, NASA made the first medical evacuation in the space station's 25 years. Now imagine that on Mars, with a 20-minute delay each way."

0:20 Problem. "Astronauts lose up to 1 to 2% of bone density every month, their muscles waste, radiation builds up, and sleep and mood suffer. NASA's own research says these hazards interact."

0:45 Solution. "AUSTROX is a 24/7 health monitor that knows where the astronaut is: Earth, orbit, Moon or Mars. It recognises how they move, forecasts bone and muscle change, tracks radiation against the career limit, and gives one clear risk score."

1:15 Demo. Open the website. Switch ISS to Mars, move the mission-day slider, toggle exercise, then change walking speed on the 3D skeleton and submit the self-check.

1:45 Difference and ask. "Continuous, location-aware, astronaut-first and offline-ready. It supports NASA's move to personalised medicine, which the Twins Study called for. Scan the QR code and try it."

F3. Likely judge questions

Is the data real? The evidence and model constants come from NASA and peer-reviewed sources. Live values are simulated for the demo, and the site says so. The design is made for real wearables.

How is this different from existing monitoring? It is continuous, location-aware, personal-baseline based and astronaut-facing, and it adds movement analysis as a daily biomarker.

How would it work without ground contact? The on-board AI is designed to run offline and sync summaries when the link is available.

How accurate are the forecasts? They are illustrative and scaled from published rates. Validation against ISS and bed-rest datasets is our next step.

What about privacy? Medical data is private. In a real deployment, data would stay on board by default and be shared with flight surgeons under NASA's medical confidentiality rules.

Why does it matter on Earth? The same bone, muscle and mobility monitoring helps with ageing, rehabilitation and remote patients.

F4. Submission checklist

  • Project title, short summary (A2) and full description (A3).
  • Live link and QR code: https://austrox.netlify.app.
  • Presentation PDF with the QR code on the last slide.
  • Transparency statement (F1).
  • List of NASA and public sources (Part G).
  • Team name: Team AUSTROX, and team member names and roles.
  • Optional: a short demo video following the pitch script.
